stem: In an investigation, which variable does the experimenter deliberately change?

options.content: the independent variable
options.rationale: It is chosen and changed by the experimenter.

options.content: the dependent variable
options.rationale: This is the variable that is measured.

options.content: a control variable
options.rationale: Control variables are kept the same.

options.content: a random variable
options.rationale: This is not one of the planned variables.

explanation: The independent variable is changed on purpose; the dependent variable is measured; control variables are kept constant.

stem: Sipho investigates how the concentration of hydrochloric acid affects the time taken for a marble chip to dissolve. What is the dependent variable?

options.content: the time taken for the marble chip to dissolve
options.rationale: This is what he measures.

options.content: the concentration of the hydrochloric acid
options.rationale: This is the independent variable: he changes it.

options.content: the mass of the marble chip
options.rationale: This should be kept the same: it is a control variable.

options.content: the temperature of the acid
options.rationale: This should also be controlled.

explanation: The dependent variable is the one measured to see the effect of the change: here, the time for the chip to dissolve.

stem: Which hazard label should be on a bottle of ethanol?

options.content: corrosive
options.rationale: Ethanol does not attack skin or metals like a concentrated acid.

options.content: oxidising
options.rationale: Ethanol is a fuel, not an oxidising agent.

options.content: radioactive
options.rationale: Ethanol is not radioactive.

options.content: flammable
options.rationale: Ethanol vapour catches fire easily.

explanation: Ethanol is highly flammable, so it must be kept away from naked flames; it is heated with a water bath, not a Bunsen burner.

stem: True or false: repeating each measurement and calculating a mean makes the results more reliable.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct: repeats show whether results agree and help to identify anomalous values.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true: repeating allows anomalies to be spotted and a mean to be calculated.

explanation: Repeated measurements that agree give confidence in a result. An anomalous result can be identified and left out of the mean.

stem: Match each substance with its main hazard.
explanation: Concentrated sulfuric acid is corrosive; paraffin is flammable; chlorine is toxic (use a fume cupboard); copper compounds harm aquatic life, so the waste is collected rather than poured down the sink.

stem: Rudo investigates how temperature affects the rate of reaction between magnesium and dilute acid. Which variable must she keep the same?

options.content: the temperature of the acid
options.rationale: This is the independent variable.

options.content: the concentration of the acid
options.rationale: Concentration also affects rate, so it must be controlled.

options.content: the time taken for the magnesium to react
options.rationale: This is the dependent variable.

options.content: the rate of the reaction
options.rationale: This is what the experiment finds out.

explanation: Any factor other than temperature that affects the rate, such as acid concentration and volume and the mass or surface area of magnesium, must be kept constant.

stem: Tendai investigates how the size of marble chips affects the rate of reaction with dilute hydrochloric acid, collecting the gas in a gas syringe. Select **all** the variables he must control.

options.content: the total mass of marble chips
options.rationale: More marble would give more gas.

options.content: the volume of acid
options.rationale: The amount of acid affects how much reacts.

options.content: the concentration of acid
options.rationale: Concentration affects the rate.

options.content: the temperature
options.rationale: Temperature affects the rate.

options.content: the size of the marble chips
options.rationale: This is the independent variable.

options.content: the volume of gas collected every 30 seconds
options.rationale: This is the dependent variable.

options.content: the rate of reaction
options.rationale: This is what is being found out.

explanation: Everything that affects the rate except chip size must be kept constant: mass of marble, volume and concentration of acid, and temperature. Chip size is changed and the gas volume is measured.
hints: Control variables are neither the thing changed nor the thing measured.

stem: Which is a sensible precaution when heating a liquid in a test tube?

options.content: Heat the bottom of the tube strongly without moving it.
options.rationale: This can make the liquid boil suddenly and shoot out.

options.content: Seal the tube with a bung before heating it.
options.rationale: Pressure could build up and blow the bung out or crack the tube.

options.content: Point it away from people and heat gently, moving the tube.
options.rationale: This prevents the liquid spitting out at anyone.

options.content: Fill the tube right to the top before heating it.
options.rationale: A full tube is more likely to spill and spit.

explanation: A test tube should be no more than about one-third full, heated gently near the liquid surface and moved in the flame, with its mouth pointing away from everyone.

stem: When dilute hydrochloric acid is added to aqueous sodium thiosulfate, a pale yellow precipitate of sulfur slowly forms, so that a cross drawn on paper under the flask disappears. Plan an investigation into how the temperature of the sodium thiosulfate solution affects the rate of this reaction.

rejected.feedback: The time for the cross to disappear is what you measure: that is the dependent variable.
The time for the cross to disappear is what you measure: that is the dependent variable.

options.content: the volume of hydrochloric acid
options.rationale: This is controlled.

options.content: the temperature of the solution
options.rationale: This is the independent variable.

options.content: the time taken for the cross to disappear
options.rationale: This is measured at each temperature.

options.content: the size of the cross
options.rationale: The same cross is used every time: a control.

parts.label: (c)

points.description: Volume and/or concentration of sodium thiosulfate solution
Volume and/or concentration of hydrochloric acid (or the same cross/flask, same depth of solution)

parts.explanation: Keep the volume and concentration of sodium thiosulfate solution the same, and the volume and concentration of hydrochloric acid the same. Use the same flask and the same cross each time.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Describe how you would carry out the investigation.

points.description: Measure a fixed volume of sodium thiosulfate (e.g. 50 cm³) with a measuring cylinder into a conical flask on a paper cross
Warm it to a chosen temperature in a water bath and record the temperature with a thermometer
Add a fixed volume of acid (e.g. 5 cm³), start the stop-watch, and stop it when the cross can no longer be seen from above
Repeat at at least five temperatures (e.g. 20–60 °C), repeating each and calculating a mean time

parts.explanation: Measure 50 cm³ of sodium thiosulfate solution with a measuring cylinder into a conical flask standing on a cross drawn on paper. Warm the flask in a water bath until the solution reaches the chosen temperature, measured with a thermometer. Add 5 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid, swirl and start the stop-watch at once. Look down through the solution and stop the watch when the cross disappears. Repeat at 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 °C, doing each temperature twice or three times and calculating the mean time.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: State one hazard and a precaution.

points.description: Sulfur dioxide (toxic/irritating gas) is produced: work in a well-ventilated room or fume cupboard; or acid is an irritant: wear eye protection; or hot water: handle with care

parts.explanation: The reaction gives off sulfur dioxide, a toxic gas, so the room should be well ventilated (or a fume cupboard used); wear eye protection because the acid is an irritant.

explanation: Temperature is changed, the time for the cross to disappear is measured, and the volumes and concentrations of both solutions are controlled. A good method uses a water bath, at least five temperatures and repeats. Sulfur dioxide is produced, so ventilation is needed.
hints: What will you change, what will you measure and what must stay the same?
Include quantities and apparatus in the method.

(a).text: the time taken for the cross to disappear at each temperature

stem: A school near Bulawayo has three water supplies: a borehole, the town tap and a river. Plan an experiment, using soap solution, to find which water sample is the hardest. [6]

points.description: Measure the same volume of each water sample (e.g. 25.0 cm³ with a pipette or measuring cylinder) into a conical flask
Add soap solution from a burette in small portions (e.g. 1.0 cm³ at a time)
Stopper and shake for the same time after each addition
Record the volume of soap solution needed to give a lather that lasts (e.g. 30 s)
Keep the soap solution and the shaking the same; repeat for each sample and take a mean
The sample needing the most soap solution is the hardest

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Use a pipette to put 25.0 cm³ of the borehole water into a conical flask. Fill a burette with soap solution. Add 1.0 cm³ of soap solution, stopper the flask and shake it for 10 seconds. Keep adding 1.0 cm³ portions, shaking the same way each time, until a lather forms that lasts for 30 seconds, and record the total volume of soap solution added. Repeat with the tap water and the river water, using the same soap solution and the same shaking method, and do each sample twice to get a mean. The water that needs the largest volume of soap solution to form a lasting lather is the hardest.

explanation: Hard water reacts with soap to form scum, so more soap is needed before a lather forms. A fair comparison keeps the volume of water, the soap solution and the shaking the same.
hints: Hard water needs more soap before it forms a lasting lather.
What must be kept the same for each sample?

stem: Why should an investigation use at least five different values of the independent variable?

options.content: so that the whole experiment finishes more quickly
options.rationale: More values take longer.

options.content: to make the experiment safer for the student doing it
options.rationale: The number of values does not affect safety.

options.content: so that the control variables can be changed as well
options.rationale: Control variables must stay the same.

options.content: so that a trend shows and a reliable line can be drawn
options.rationale: Few points cannot show the shape of a relationship.

explanation: With only two or three values you cannot tell whether a relationship is a straight line or a curve. Five or more values spread across a range show the trend clearly.
hints: Think about drawing a graph of the results.

stem: A student's plan says: 'Add some acid to some marble chips and time how long it takes.' Which improvement is most important?

options.content: Use a much bigger beaker so that nothing spills over.
options.rationale: This does not make the plan clearer or fairer.

options.content: State the volume and concentration of acid and the mass of chips.
options.rationale: Without quantities the experiment cannot be repeated fairly.

options.content: Use a different, stronger acid for the whole reaction.
options.rationale: The type of acid is not the problem.

options.content: Do the experiment outside, where it is cooler and safer.
options.rationale: This does not improve the plan.

explanation: A plan must give quantities and apparatus so that the test is fair and can be repeated: for example, 2.0 g of marble chips and 25 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid measured with a measuring cylinder.
hints: Could someone else repeat this experiment exactly?

stem: Complete the sentences about variables.

payload.template: The variable that is measured is the {{blank:dep}} variable. Variables kept the same throughout are {{blank:con}} variables.

explanation: The dependent variable is measured; control variables are kept constant; the independent variable is changed.

stem: Chipo makes copper(II) sulfate crystals by warming dilute sulfuric acid with excess copper(II) oxide, filtering, and heating the filtrate to evaporate some of the water.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Copper(II) sulfate is labelled 'harmful to the environment'. What should Chipo do with the leftover solution?

options.content: Pour it down the sink with plenty of water.
options.rationale: Dilution does not remove the copper from the water system.

options.content: Pour it onto the school garden.
options.rationale: This would contaminate the soil.

options.content: Pour it into a labelled waste container.
options.rationale: Copper compounds harm aquatic life and must not enter drains.

options.content: Leave it in an open beaker on the bench.
options.rationale: This is unsafe and does not dispose of it.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Give two other safety precautions for this experiment, with a reason for each.

points.description: Wear eye protection because the acid / hot solution can splash or spit
Heat gently / stop heating when crystals start to form, because the solution can spit; or let apparatus cool before handling

parts.explanation: Wear eye protection, because dilute sulfuric acid is an irritant and hot solution may spit during evaporation. Heat the evaporating basin gently and stop when crystals first appear, so the solution does not spit or overheat, and let the basin cool before touching it.

explanation: Heavy-metal compounds such as copper(II) sulfate go into a waste container, not down the sink. Eye protection and gentle heating protect against splashes and spitting.
hints: Precautions should match a named hazard.

stem: True or false: in a fair test, several variables are changed at the same time so that the experiment finishes faster.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: If several variables change at once, you cannot tell which one caused the effect. Change only the independent variable.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct: only one variable (the independent variable) is changed in a fair test.

explanation: A fair test changes only the independent variable, so any change in the dependent variable can be linked to it.
hints: How would you know which change caused the effect?

stem: Prediction: 'The higher the concentration of acid, the shorter the time for a piece of magnesium ribbon to react.' Which set of results supports the prediction?

options.content: 0.5 mol/dm³: 120 s; 1.0 mol/dm³: 62 s; 2.0 mol/dm³: 31 s
options.rationale: The time falls as the concentration rises.

options.content: 0.5 mol/dm³: 31 s; 1.0 mol/dm³: 62 s; 2.0 mol/dm³: 120 s
options.rationale: The time rises as the concentration rises: the opposite.

options.content: 0.5 mol/dm³: 60 s; 1.0 mol/dm³: 61 s; 2.0 mol/dm³: 60 s
options.rationale: No change: concentration seems to have no effect.

options.content: 0.5 mol/dm³: 60 s; 1.0 mol/dm³: 120 s; 2.0 mol/dm³: 30 s
options.rationale: No consistent trend.

explanation: The prediction says time should decrease as concentration increases. Only the first set shows that pattern.

stem: A student plans to find how temperature affects the rate of reaction between marble chips and dilute hydrochloric acid. Her plan: 'Heat some acid with a Bunsen burner to different temperatures. Add a handful of marble chips each time (whatever sizes are in the jar). Time how long the fizzing lasts. Do each temperature once.'

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Identify two weaknesses in this plan.

points.description: Marble chips are of different sizes/masses each time (surface area and mass not controlled), so it is not a fair test
Quantities of acid not stated / temperature not measured or kept constant / only one reading at each temperature (no repeats) / end of fizzing is hard to judge

parts.explanation: The size and mass of marble chips change each time, so surface area is not controlled and the test is unfair. The volume and concentration of acid are not given, the temperature is not measured or kept steady, each temperature is done only once and 'when the fizzing stops' is hard to judge.

parts.label: (b)

points.description: Use the same mass (e.g. 2.0 g) of marble chips of the same size each time
Use a fixed volume and concentration of acid, a thermometer and water bath, repeat each temperature, and/or measure gas volume in a set time with a gas syringe

parts.explanation: Use 2.0 g of chips of the same size each time with 25 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ acid; heat the acid in a water bath and check the temperature with a thermometer; repeat each temperature three times; and measure the volume of gas collected in a gas syringe in the first 60 seconds instead of judging when fizzing stops.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Which apparatus is best for keeping the acid at each chosen temperature?

options.content: a Bunsen burner under the flask
options.rationale: The temperature keeps rising and is not controlled.

options.content: an ice bath only
options.rationale: This only gives low temperatures.

options.content: a measuring cylinder
options.rationale: This measures volume, not temperature.

options.content: a thermostatically controlled water bath
options.rationale: It keeps a steady, known temperature.

explanation: The plan is unfair (chip size and mass vary), lacks quantities and temperature control, and has no repeats. Fixed quantities, a water bath with a thermometer, repeats and a clear measurement such as gas volume in a set time fix these problems.
hints: Look for variables that are not controlled and measurements that are vague.

stem: Zinc reacts with dilute acid to release hydrogen. A student wants to follow the rate by measuring either the volume of hydrogen (gas syringe) or the loss in mass of the flask (balance reading to 0.01 g). Which method is better, and why?

options.content: Balance, because masses are always more accurate than volumes.
options.rationale: The mass change here would be too small to measure well.

options.content: Gas syringe, because hydrogen is too dense to escape the flask.
options.rationale: Hydrogen is the least dense gas and escapes easily.

options.content: Gas syringe: the mass of hydrogen lost is too small to weigh accurately.
options.rationale: A few hundred cm³ of hydrogen has a mass of only a few hundredths of a gram.

options.content: Balance, because hydrogen would dissolve in the gas syringe.
options.rationale: Gases do not dissolve in a syringe.

explanation: Hydrogen has a molar mass of only 2 g/mol: 240 cm³ (0.01 mol) has a mass of 0.02 g. That change is too small for a 0.01 g balance to follow accurately, so collecting the gas in a syringe is better. (Mass loss works well for carbon dioxide, which is much heavier.)
hints: Work out roughly the mass of 240 cm³ of hydrogen.

stem: Name the safety equipment that should be worn to protect the eyes during practical work.
explanation: Safety goggles (or safety glasses / spectacles) protect the eyes from splashes of acids, alkalis and hot liquids.

stem: Which of these experiments should be carried out in a fume cupboard?

options.content: dissolving sodium chloride in water
options.rationale: No harmful gas is produced.

options.content: preparing a small sample of chlorine gas
options.rationale: Chlorine is a toxic gas.

options.content: weighing marble chips
options.rationale: There is no hazard that needs a fume cupboard.

options.content: measuring the temperature of tap water
options.rationale: This is harmless.

explanation: A fume cupboard removes toxic or irritating gases such as chlorine, sulfur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide, so they are not breathed in.
